summary.tldr: Clarifies when an employer may be seen as dominating a trade union, lets the labour board revoke certification, and adds penalties under the Canada Labour Code.
what_it_does: Prohibits the Board from certifying a trade union, or treating its agreement as a collective agreement, if the union is dominated or influenced by an employer or someone acting for an employer.
Requires the Board to be satisfied that a union is not dominated or influenced, and is governed by members elected by the employees it wants to represent, before certifying it.

Lets employees ask to revoke a union’s certification if they claim employer domination or influence. The Board must hold an inquiry if 25% of employees in the unit apply in writing, and must revoke certification if it finds domination or influence.
Bars those revocation applications during an allowed strike or lockout involving the employees, unless the Board consents, and applies similar revocation rules to councils of trade unions.
Makes employer domination or influence an offence punishable on summary conviction by a fine of up to $100,000.

Allows regulations to create administrative monetary penalties for breaches of section 94, and requires the Minister of Labour to review the new provisions within five years and table a report in Parliament.
summary.background: The bill amends the Canada Labour Code. It adds a definition of when an employer or someone acting for an employer dominates or influences a trade union.
